claim: Over 200,000 older Americans currently suffer from chronic age-associated fibrotic lung disease annually.
source: Over 200,000 older Americans currently suffer from chronic age-associated fibrotic lung disease (Cordier and Cottin, 2013; Lederer and Martinez, 2018; Richeldi et al., 2017) annually (Hecker, 2018; Lederer and Martinez, 2018; Martinez et al., 2017; Raghu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Alveolar epithelial cell damage, proliferation of fibroblasts and extracellular matrix accumulation lead to irreversible disruption of the lung architecture in IPF.
source: Alveolar epithelial cell damage, proliferation of fibroblasts and extracellular matrix (ECM) accumulation lead to irreversible disruption of the lung architecture (Kinoshita and Goto, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The etiology of IPF remains unknown.
source: While the etiology of IPF remains unknown, there is an ongoing need for understanding mechanisms of disease and diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers of disease (Drakopanagiotakis et al., 2018; Tzouvelekis et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Extracellular vesicles, including exosomes and microvesicles, are potential candidates for elucidation of a biomarker signature for IPF and other fibrotic diseases.
source: Extracellular vesicles (EVs), including exosomes and microvesicles, are potential candidates for elucidation of a biomarker signature for IPF and other fibrotic diseases (H Rashed et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: EVs deliver miRNAs, mRNA, and tRNA into target cells as a key component of cell-cell communication.
source: As a key component of cell–cell communication, EVs deliver miRNAs, mRNA, and tRNA into target cells (Yáñez-Mó et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The systemic distribution of EVs in body fluids may reflect the presence of disease.
source: In addition, their systemic distribution in body fluids may reflect the presence of disease.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the properties of EVs.

claim: Exosomes are present in most body fluids, including blood, breast milk, saliva, urine, bile, pancreatic juice, cerebrospinal, and peritoneal fluids.
source: The ease of collection and presence of exosomes in most body fluids, including blood, breast milk, saliva, urine, bile, pancreatic juice, cerebrospinal, and peritoneal fluids, have facilitated recent studies investigating their use as diagnostic and prognostic markers of disease (Keller et al., 2011; Raposo and Stoorvogel, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Exosomes are released by all cells and contain cargo from the cell of origin.
source: Because exosomes are released by all cells and contain cargo from the cell of origin, it is conceivable that they deliver pathogenic materials leading to a disease phenotype.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about exosomes.

claim: Molecular analysis of lung biopsies from individuals with IPF reveal a unique miRNA transcriptome compared with the miRNA transcriptome found from non-fibrotic lung biopsy samples.
source: Molecular analysis of lung biopsies from individuals with IPF reveal a unique miRNA transcriptome compared with the miRNA transcriptome found from non-fibrotic lung biopsy samples providing evidence supporting the disease conferring properties of exosomes (Guiot et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In serum isolated from individuals with IPF compared to control serum samples, there were 47 differentially expressed miRNAs.
source: In serum isolated from individuals with IPF compared to control serum samples, there were 47 differentially expressed miRNAs (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Njock et al. reported a signature of miR-142–3 p, miR-33a-5p, miR-let-7d-5p in sputum of individuals with IPF.
source: Njock et al. reported a signature of miR-142–3 p, miR-33a-5p, miR-let-7d-5p in sputum of individuals with IPF (Njock et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In lung tissue EVs isolated from mouse alveolar spaces and IPF lungs, TGF-β and Wnt signaling were increased after bleomycin treatment.
source: Parimon et al. found that in lung tissue EVs isolated from mouse alveolar spaces and IPF lungs, TGF-β and Wnt signaling were increased after bleomycin (Bleo) treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Parimon et al.).

claim: There are no published studies using exosomes from urine of individuals with IPF or any urine-derived exosomes in the investigation of fibrotic lung disease.
source: To the best of our knowledge, there are no published studies using exosomes from urine of individuals with IPF (U-IPFexo) or any urine-derived exosomes in the investigation of fibrotic lung disease.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: U-IPFexo cargo could promote a fibrotic phenotype.
source: In the present study we isolated and characterized exosomes isolated from the urine of 16 male individuals with IPF and 10 age and sex-matched control individuals to test the hypothesis that U-IPFexo cargo could promote a fibrotic phenotype.
evidence: This is the hypothesis being tested in the study.

claim: A fibrotic miRNA expression pattern was found in serum and urine derived from the same individual with IPF.
source: We found a a fibrotic miRNA expression pattern in serum and urine derved from the same individual with IPF.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Several miRNAs previously reported in the lung, serum, and sputum from individuals with IPF could be identified in urine, lung, and serum IPFexo.
source: Our results also confirmed that several miRNAs previously reported in the lung, serum, and sputum from individuals with IPF (Njock et al., 2019; Pandit and Milosevic, 2015; Rajasekaran et al., 2015) could be identified in urine, lung, and serum IPFexo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study and citations to published literature.

claim: Intravenous infusion of urine exosomes isolated from both normal and diseased individuals revealed fairly rapid biodistribution to the lung.
source: Intravenous infusion of urine exosomes isolated from both normal and diseased individuals using in vivo bioluminescent imaging system, revealed fairly rapid biodistribution to the lung.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study using in vivo bioluminescent imaging.

claim: U-IPFexo conveyed a pro-fibrotic lung phenotype in ex vivo human and mouse lung punch studies.
source: Ex vivo human and mouse lung punch studies and in vivo mouse models were used to functionally assess the effect of tissue (lungs) and systemic (urine and serum) exosomes isolated from individuals with IPF and 'control' exosomes isolated from urine and fibroblasts from control lungs (Habermann et al., 2019). U-IPFexo conveyed a pro-fibrotic lung phenotype and inhibited skin tissue repair.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from ex vivo lung punch studies.

claim: U-IPFexo inhibited skin tissue repair.
source: U-IPFexo conveyed a pro-fibrotic lung phenotype and inhibited skin tissue repair.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Body weight is independently associated with survival of individuals with IPF.
source: Since body weight is independently associated with survival of individuals with IPF, we used body weight as a surrogate for stage of disease and found that mice lost more body weight after treatment with U-IPFexo than with Bleo treatment alone (Mogulkoc et al., 2018; Nakatsuka et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mice lost more body weight after treatment with U-IPFexo than with Bleo treatment alone.
source: Since body weight is independently associated with survival of individuals with IPF, we used body weight as a surrogate for stage of disease and found that mice lost more body weight after treatment with U-IPFexo than with Bleo treatment alone (Mogulkoc et al., 2018; Nakatsuka et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Mice receiving exosomes from subjects with non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis or asthma did not exhibit changes in fibrotic markers.
source: We also included urine exosomes from subjects with non-cystic fibrosis (non-CF) bronchiectasis or asthma (non-fibrotic lung diseases) in in vivo experiments. Mice receiving these exosomes did not exhibit changes in fibrotic markers.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Markers of lung fibrosis are specific and may be detected systemically, outside of the lung.
source: These findings suggest that markers of lung fibrosis are specific, may be detected systemically, outside of the lung, and can communicate the pathology to different tissues.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Markers of lung fibrosis can communicate the pathology to different tissues.
source: These findings suggest that markers of lung fibrosis are specific, may be detected systemically, outside of the lung, and can communicate the pathology to different tissues.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: Urine exosomes have the potential to be used as disease-defining biomarkers in patients with IPF.
source: Importantly, urine exosomes have the potential to be used as disease-defining biomarkers in patients with IPF.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the study findings.

claim: Random urine samples were collected from male control individuals (ages 55–77) or individuals seen in the Interstitial Lung Disease clinic at the University of Miami Hospital.
source: Random urine samples were collected (between 10am-2pm) from male control individuals (ages 55–77) or individuals seen in the Interstitial Lung Disease (ILD, subjects with IPF ages 55–79; subjects with non-CF bronchiectasis ages 73–86; and subjects with asthma ages 36–61) clinic at the University of Miami Hospital.
evidence: The claim describes the methods used in the study.

claim: Written informed consent was obtained from the participants with an approved Institutional Review Board protocol (IRB# 20060249) at the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine.
source: Written informed consent was obtained from the participants with an approved Institutional Review Board protocol (IRB# 20060249) at the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine.
evidence: The claim describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Control urines were obtained from subjects that did not have underlying kidney, heart, or lung comorbidities and had normal albumin creatinine ratios.
source: Control urines were obtained from subjects that did not have underlying kidney, heart, or lung comorbidities and had normal albumin creatinine ratios sampled in an aliquot of each urine.
evidence: The claim describes the selection criteria for control subjects.

claim: Patients with known kidney disease or diabetes were excluded from the study.
source: Patients with known kidney disease or diabetes were excluded from the study and a small aliquot of urine was used to measure urine albumin and creatinine to exclude samples with albuminuria (Creatinine LiquiColor Test, Stanbio Laboratory Boerne, TX and albumin Elisa, Bethyl laboratories, Montgomery, TX).
evidence: The claim describes the exclusion criteria for the study.

claim: Samples were selected for inclusion in the present study after review of imaging confirming a definitive UIP pattern.
source: Samples were selected for inclusion in the present study after review of imaging confirming a definitive UIP pattern (Raghu et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim describes the selection criteria for IPF samples.

claim: Exosome size from urine, blood and cells was approximately 30–150 µm.
source: Exosome size from urine, blood and cells was approximately 30–150 µm.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: EM performed on isolated exosomes confirmed a size and shape previously reported for exosomes.
source: EM performed on isolated exosomes (Figure 2) confirmed a size and shape previously reported for exosomes (Gurunathan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by EM data shown in Figure 2 and citation to published literature.

claim: The presence of exosome markers CD1, CDC9, and CD63 were determined by MACSPlex analysis.
source: The presence of exosome markers CD1, CDC9, and CD63 were determined by MACSPlex analysis and CD63 (Figure 2B) was confirmed by western analysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from MACSPlex analysis and western blot shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Other exosome markers present were CD9 and CD81.
source: Other exosome markers present were CD9 and CD81.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: U-IPFexo relative expression analysis revealed dysregulated expression of miR-let-7D, miR-199, miR-29, and miR-181 compared to urine-derived control exosomes.
source: U-IPFexo relative expression analysis revealed dysregulated expression of miR-let-7D, miR-199, miR-29, and miR-181 (Figure 3A, B, C and D, Figure 3—source data 1) compared to urine-derived control exosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Serum-derived exosome miRNA and urine-derived exosomal miRNA from the same patient showed no difference in relative expression of selected miRNAs.
source: We compared serum-derived exosome miRNA to urine-derived exosomal miRNA from the same patient and found no difference in relative expression of selected miRNAs (Figure 3E, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Selected miRNAs have been shown to be altered in lung tissue and serum from individuals with IPF.
source: These selected miRNAs have also been shown to be altered in lung tissue and serum from individuals with IPF (Casanova et al., 2021; Omote and Sauler, 2020; Ortiz-Quintero et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Cargo carried in urine exosomes from individuals with IPF may parallel cargo of serum-derived exosomes in the same individual.
source: These data suggest that cargo carried in urine exosomes from individuals with IPF may parallel cargo of serum-derived exosomes in the same individual.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Pure exosome preparations do not contain detectable mRNA expression of TGFβ, IGF or ER subtypes.
source: As expected in pure exosome preparations (Batagov and Kurochkin, 2013), we did not detect mRNA expression of TGFβ, IGF or ER subtypes from normal or diseased exosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation to published literature.

claim: Exosomes were located in the lung within 5 min post-tail vein injection regardless of source.
source: Regardless of source (U-IPFexo or control exosomes), exosomes were located in the lung within 5 min post-tail vein injection.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo bioluminescent imaging.

claim: All mice injected with U-IPFexo had a higher lung signal over time compared to mice injected with urine-derived age and sex-matched controls.
source: All mice injected with U-IPFexo had a higher lung signal over time compared to mice injected with urine-derived age and sex-matched controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A ), suggesting that these exosomes may be retained longer in the lung than control exosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: U-IPFexo may be retained longer in the lung than control exosomes.
source: All mice injected with U-IPFexo had a higher lung signal over time compared to mice injected with urine-derived age and sex-matched controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A ), suggesting that these exosomes may be retained longer in the lung than control exosomes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: The lung signal evident at 30 min was not evident at 48 hr suggesting clearance of the exosomes.
source: A set of mice sacrificed at 48 hr to quantify signals in heart/lung, spleen, liver, and kidney (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) showed that the lung signal evident at 30 min (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) was not evident at 48 hr as seen by IVIS suggesting clearance of the exosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: Exosomes labeled with nanoparticles were visualized in mouse lung punches by TEM.
source: Utilizing TEM, exosomes labeled with nanoparticles were visualized in mouse lung punches (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) injected with urine-derived control exosomes (Figure 5A-C) or U-IPFexo (Figure 5D-H).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5.

claim: TEM revealed increased collagen bands in punches injected with U-IPFexo.
source: TEM revealed increased collagen bands in those punches injected with U-IPFexo (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Lung structure was preserved in both normal and U-IPF treated samples.
source: Lung structure was preserved in both normal and U-IPF treated samples.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from TEM.

claim: Immunofluorescent staining of punches appeared to have decreased surfactant protein C positive cells (AEC II) after treatment with IPF derived exosomes compared to treatment with control exosomes.
source: Immunofluorescent staining of punches appeared to have decreased surfactant protein C positive cells (AEC II) after treatment with IPF derived exosomes (Figure 6C) compared to treatment with control exosomes (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Exosomes are taken up by alveolar cells.
source: Taken together these data suggest that exosomes are taken up by the alveolar cells and that IPFexo may promote disease by inhibiting the reparative AEC II cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: IPFexo may promote disease by inhibiting the reparative AEC II cells.
source: Taken together these data suggest that exosomes are taken up by the alveolar cells and that IPFexo may promote disease by inhibiting the reparative AEC II cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: αv-integrin and collagen type I mRNA increased after injection with MF-IPFexo compared to control in human lung punches.
source: αv-integrin and collagen type I mRNA increased after injection with MF-IPFexo compared to control (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Cav-1 protein decreased after U-IPFexo were injected into human lung punches.
source: Consistent with our published data in the lungs of mice with Bleo-injury and lung tissue from individuals with IPF (Elliot et al., 2019; Rubio et al., 2018), Cav-1 protein decreased (Figure 7B,Figure 7—source data 1) and ERα protein expression increased (Figure 7C, Figure 7—source data 1) after U-IPFexo were injected into human lung punches.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and citations to published literature.

claim: ERα protein expression increased after U-IPFexo were injected into human lung punches.
source: Consistent with our published data in the lungs of mice with Bleo-injury and lung tissue from individuals with IPF (Elliot et al., 2019; Rubio et al., 2018), Cav-1 protein decreased (Figure 7B,Figure 7—source data 1) and ERα protein expression increased (Figure 7C, Figure 7—source data 1) after U-IPFexo were injected into human lung punches.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and citations to published literature.

claim: Markers for fibrosis (αv-integrin, collagen type I mRNA expression) were only activated by the U-IPFexo and not control exosomes or PBS alone in mouse lung punches.
source: Markers for fibrosis (αv-integrin, collagen type I mRNA expression) and other downstream fibrotic pathways (ERα, c-Jun, AKT expression and MMP-9 activity) were only activated by the U-IPFexo and not control exosomes or PBS alone (Figure 7D–I, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D-I.

claim: Other downstream fibrotic pathways (ERα, c-Jun, AKT expression and MMP-9 activity) were only activated by the U-IPFexo and not control exosomes or PBS alone in mouse lung punches.
source: Markers for fibrosis (αv-integrin, collagen type I mRNA expression) and other downstream fibrotic pathways (ERα, c-Jun, AKT expression and MMP-9 activity) were only activated by the U-IPFexo and not control exosomes or PBS alone (Figure 7D–I, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D-I.

claim: TGFβ mRNA expression increased 2.5 fold in punches that were injected with IPF exosomes compared to those injected with PBS or control exosome injections.
source: We found a 2.5 fold increase in TGFβ mRNA expression in punches that were injected with IPF exosomes compared to those injected with PBS or control exosome injections (p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: mRNA expression of αv-integrin and collagen type I were increased in punches injected with MF-IPFexo compared with punches injected with age and sex-matched control fibroblast exosomes.
source: mRNA expression of αv-integrin and collagen type I were increased in punches injected with MF-IPFexo compared with punches injected with age and sex-matched control fibroblast exosomes (Figure 7J, K, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7J and K.

claim: ERα protein expression was increased after injection of U-IPFexo (1.4 fold increase over control, p=0.05) and MF-IPFexo (>3 fold) into lung punches compared to control exosomes.
source: ERα protein expression shown to be upregulated in the lung tissue and myofibroblasts isolated from individuals with IPF (Elliot et al., 2019) was increased after injection of U-IPFexo (1.4 fold increase over control, p=0.05) and MF-IPFexo (>3 fold) into lung punches (Figure 7F and L, Figure 7—source data 1) compared to control exosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F and L and citation to published literature.

claim: Increased c-Jun expression was noted after injection of IPF exosomes but not after injection with control exosomes.
source: Finally, increased c-Jun expression was noted after injection of IPF exosomes but not after injection with control exosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: U-IPFexo stimulate a fibrotic pathway response like that stimulated by MF-IPFexo.
source: U-IPFexo stimulate a fibrotic pathway response like that stimulated by MF-IPFexo.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: U-IPFexo treatment delayed wound healing in human ex vivo skin wound healing assay.
source: U-IPFexo treatment delayed would healing mirroring our previous data showing that mice who develop pulmonary fibrosis after treatment with Bleo also demonstrate a delay in wound healing (Rubio et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study and citation to published literature.

claim: U-IPFexo decreased wound closure compared to control exosomes or PBS (27 ± 6.3% vs 14 ± 0.7%, vs 95%).
source: We found that U-IPFexo decreased wound closure compared to control exosomes or PBS (27 ± 6.3% vs 14 ± 0.7%, vs 95%, n=3 technical replicates from two to three biological exosome isolates/group, Figure 8, Figure 8—source data 1), suggesting that exosomes carry a disease phenotype that can impair tissue repair.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Exosomes carry a disease phenotype that can impair tissue repair.
source: We found that U-IPFexo decreased wound closure compared to control exosomes or PBS (27 ± 6.3% vs 14 ± 0.7%, vs 95%, n=3 technical replicates from two to three biological exosome isolates/group, Figure 8, Figure 8—source data 1), suggesting that exosomes carry a disease phenotype that can impair tissue repair.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Decreased expression of miR-29 and miR-let-7d was found in punches treated with U-IPFexo or MF-IPFexo.
source: We found decreased expression of miR-29 and miR-let-7d in punches treated with U-IPFexo (Table 4) or MF-IPFexo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 4.

claim: MiR-199 was upregulated in punches injected with U-IPFexo, but remained unchanged by MF-IPFexo.
source: MiR-199 was upregulated in those punches injected with U-IPFexo, but remained unchanged by MF-IPFexo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Increased miR-199 expression correlates with downregulated Cav-1 expression.
source: We and others have previously shown an increase in miR-199 expression in IPF lung tissue and cells and that increased miR-199 expression correlates with downregulated Cav-1 expression (Aranda et al., 2015; Rubio et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Punch expression of miR-34a, and miR-142 was regulated in a manner similar to expression found in isolated exosomes after treatment with either U-IPFexo or MF-IPFexo.
source: Punch expression of miR-34a, and miR-142 was regulated in a manner similar to expression found in isolated exosomes after treatment with either U-IPFexo or MF-IPFexo, supporting the relevance of the cargo carried in urine of individuals with IPF (Shetty et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study and citation to published literature.

claim: Analysis of lung tissue obtained from Bleo treated mice sacrificed at day 21 showed a higher Ashcroft score in those mice receiving U-IPFexo compared to control exosomes or Bleo alone.
source: Analysis of lung tissue obtained from Bleo treated mice sacrificed at day 21 showed a higher Ashcroft score (Figure 9M, Figure 9—source data 1) and collagen content (Figure 9N, Figure 9—source data 1) in those mice receiving U-IPFexo compared to control exosomes or Bleo alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9M.

claim: Analysis of lung tissue obtained from Bleo treated mice sacrificed at day 21 showed higher collagen content in those mice receiving U-IPFexo compared to control exosomes or Bleo alone.
source: Analysis of lung tissue obtained from Bleo treated mice sacrificed at day 21 showed a higher Ashcroft score (Figure 9M, Figure 9—source data 1) and collagen content (Figure 9N, Figure 9—source data 1) in those mice receiving U-IPFexo compared to control exosomes or Bleo alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9N.

claim: αV-integrin mRNA expression was higher in lungs of mice that received U-IPFexo compared to Bleo alone.
source: αV-integrin (Figure 9O, Figure 9—source data 1) mRNA expression was higher in lungs of mice that received U-IPFexo compared to Bleo alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9O.

claim: Higher TGFB mRNA expression was noted in the lung tissue of mice injected with U-IPFexo compared to Bleo treatment alone (p>0.001, 23.8±3.9 vs 11.66±0.6).
source: We noted higher TGFB mRNA expression in the lung tissue of mice injected with U-IPFexo compared to Bleo treatment alone (p>0.001, 23.8±3.9 vs 11.66±0.6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Lungs obtained from mice treated with urine exosomes from either asthmatics or subjects with non-CF bronchiectasis exhibited increased TGFB mRNA expression.
source: Lungs obtained from mice treated with urine exosomes from either asthmatics or subjects with non-CF bronchiectasis also exhibited increased TGFB mRNA expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: MMP-2 was induced 2.5-fold by U-IPFexo (p<0.05) compared to Bleo treatment, control exosomes or other exosomes.
source: MMP-2 was induced 2.5-fold by U-IPFexo (p<0.05) compared to Bleo treatment, control exosomes or other exosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: When Bleo injury was followed by injection of U-IPFexo, fibrosis was more homogeneous and widespread compared to Bleo treatment alone.
source: When Bleo injury was followed by injection of U-IPFexo, fibrosis was more homogeneous and widespread compared to Bleo treatment alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from the study.

claim: Mice treated with Bleo +IPF exosomes lost 35±2.6% BW compared to mice treated with Bleo (29 ± 2.6% of BW; p=0.05 compared to IPF) or mice receiving Bleo +control exosomes (19 ± 3.2% of BW; p<0.05 compared to Bleo, p<0.01 compared to IPF).
source: Mice treated with Bleo +IPF exosomes lost 35±2.6% BW compared to mice treated with Bleo (29 ± 2.6% of BW; p=0.05 compared to IPF) or mice receiving Bleo +control exosomes (19 ± 3.2% of BW; p<0.05 compared to Bleo, p<0.01 compared to IPF).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Bleo-treated mice that received urine derived exosomes from individuals with non-CF bronchiectasis lost more weight (39 ± 5.7% BW; p<0.05) than Bleo-treated mice.
source: Bleo-treated mice that received urine derived exosomes from individuals with non-CF bronchiectasis lost more weight (39 ± 5.7% BW; p<0.05) than Bleo-treated mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Bleo-treated mice receiving urine derived exosomes from individuals with asthma lost a similar amount of weight as the Bleo-treated mice (27 ± 3.5% of BW).
source: The Bleo-treated mice receiving urine derived exosomes from individuals with asthma lost a similar amount of weight as the Bleo-treated mice (27 ± 3.5% of BW).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: mir-let-7d, and –142 expression decreased while miR-34a, and –199 were increased in lung tissue from Bleo mice treated with U-IPFexo.
source: We also found that mir-let-7d, and –142 expression decreased while miR-34a, and –199 were increased in lung tissue from Bleo mice treated with U-IPFexo (Table 5) but not urine exosomes derived from either asthmatics or subjects with non-CF bronchiectasis (Table 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 5.

claim: Ashcroft scoring and histology did not demonstrate changes consistent with fibrosis in lung tissue collected from naive animals treated with PBS or naive animals treated with U-IPFexo.
source: Although Ashcroft scoring and histology did not demonstrate changes consistent with fibrosis in lung tissue collected from naive animals treated with PBS or naive animals treated with U-IPFexo, increased collagen content (Figure 9—figure supplement 1, Figure 9—figure supplement 1—source data 1), and dysregulated miR-34a, miR-199 miR-29, and –142 expression (Table 5), were detected in lung tissue obtained from these mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Increased collagen content and dysregulated miR-34a, miR-199 miR-29, and –142 expression were detected in lung tissue obtained from naive mice treated with U-IPFexo.
source: Although Ashcroft scoring and histology did not demonstrate changes consistent with fibrosis in lung tissue collected from naive animals treated with PBS or naive animals treated with U-IPFexo, increased collagen content (Figure 9—figure supplement 1, Figure 9—figure supplement 1—source data 1), and dysregulated miR-34a, miR-199 miR-29, and –142 expression (Table 5), were detected in lung tissue obtained from these mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and Table 5.

claim: EVs isolated from various tissues, cells and body fluids contain bioactive molecules such as proteins, lipids, and RNAs derived from the cell of origin.
source: EVs isolated from various tissues, cells and body fluids contain bioactive molecules such as proteins, lipids, and RNAs derived from the cell of origin (Collino et al., 2010; Vizoso et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: This study is the first to report that exosomes isolated from urine of IPF patients confer a disease phenotype in vivo, in human ex vivo lung punches and impair ex vivo wound healing in mouse and human tissues.
source: Our study is the first to report that exosomes isolated from urine of IPF patients, U-IPFexo, confer a disease phenotype in vivo, in human ex vivo lung punches and impair ex vivo wound healing in mouse and human tissues.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: MF-IPFexo activated markers of fibrosis in ex vivo lung punches compared to punches treated with lung fibroblast-derived exosomes isolated from the lung tissue of age and sex-matched individuals without fibrotic lung disease.
source: In a similar manner, MF-IPFexo activated markers of fibrosis in ex vivo lung punches compared to punches treated with lung fibroblast-derived exosomes isolated from the lung tissue of age and sex-matched individuals without fibrotic lung disease.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Changes in miRNAs have been implicated in gene expression associated with the development of IPF.
source: Changes in miRNAs have been implicated in gene expression associated with the development of IPF (Njock et al., 2019; Pandit and Milosevic, 2015; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: miR-let-7, miR-29a, miR-181b, and miR-199 are known to regulate expression of pro-fibrotic, inflammatory and ECM encoding genes.
